questions.q: The reaction responsible for energy generation in the sun is —

In ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₄Si + x, the particle x is —
questions.work:
Mass numbers: 27 + 4 = 30 + A ⇒ A = 1.
Charges: 13 + 2 = 14 + Z ⇒ Z = 1. So x = ¹₁H, a proton.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) A device in which a sustained nuclear chain reaction is carried out in a controlled manner is a ______. (b) The energy of the sun is produced by nuclear ______.
Fill in the blanks: (a) ______ is an effective moderator used in nuclear reactors. (b) The fuel in most nuclear reactors is ______.
Give one word: (a) Splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei. (b) Joining of light nuclei into a heavier one.
State True or False: (a) Fusion requires a very high temperature. (b) An uncontrolled chain reaction is used in a nuclear power station.
questions.answer:
(a) True — about 10⁷ K.
(b) False — a power station uses a controlled chain reaction.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain, with a reaction, how energy is released in nuclear fission.
questions.answer: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + about 200 MeV. The total mass of the products is less than that of the reactants; the lost mass Δm appears as energy E = Δm c², because the fragments are more tightly bound.

questions.q: Out of fission and fusion, which converts mass into energy more efficiently, and why?
questions.answer: Fusion. Per unit mass of fuel it releases several times more energy (e.g. about 6.7 MeV per nucleon for hydrogen to helium, against about 0.85 MeV per nucleon for uranium fission), because light nuclei gain much more binding energy per nucleon when they fuse.

questions.q: What is a chain reaction?
questions.answer: In fission each U-235 nucleus releases 2–3 neutrons, which can split further nuclei, which release more neutrons, and so on. The reaction becomes self-sustaining and grows rapidly if not controlled.

questions.q: Why is a neutron the best projectile for nuclear reactions?
questions.answer: It has no charge, so it is not repelled by the positively charged nucleus. Even slow neutrons can enter the nucleus and cause a reaction.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: What is meant by nuclear fission and chain reaction? How is a chain reaction controlled in a nuclear reactor? Name two fissile materials.
questions.answer:
Fission: a heavy nucleus such as U-235, on absorbing a slow neutron, splits into two medium nuclei with the release of about 200 MeV and 2–3 neutrons.
Chain reaction: these neutrons cause further fissions, so the process is self-sustaining.
Control: the moderator (heavy water or graphite) slows the neutrons, and cadmium or boron control rods absorb the extra neutrons so that on average exactly one neutron per fission causes another.
Fissile materials: U-235 and Pu-239.

questions.q: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
questions.answer:
Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into lighter ones; triggered by slow neutrons at ordinary temperatures; can be controlled (reactors); produces radioactive waste.
Fusion: light nuclei combine into a heavier one; needs about 10⁷ K; occurs in the sun and stars; not yet controlled for power; gives more energy per unit mass and less radioactive waste.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe the main parts of a nuclear reactor and the function of each.
questions.answer:
(1) Fuel — U-235 or Pu-239 rods, in which fission occurs.
(2) Moderator — heavy water or graphite, which slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds so they can cause further fission.
(3) Control rods — cadmium or boron, which absorb neutrons; moving them in or out controls the rate of reaction.
(4) Coolant — water, heavy water or liquid sodium, which carries the heat to a heat exchanger to make steam that drives turbines.
(5) Shielding — thick concrete and lead walls protect workers from radiation.
The reactor keeps the chain reaction controlled so that energy is released steadily.
